Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

There once was a Square, such a square little Square, And he loved a trim Triangle; But she was a flirt and around her skirt Vainly she made him dangle. Oh he wanted to wed and he had no dread Of domestic woes and wrangles; For he thought that his fate was to procreate Cute little Squares and Triangles. Now it happened one day on that geometric way There swaggered a big bold Cube, With a haughty stare and he made that Square Have the air of a perfect boob; To his solid spell the Triangle fell, And she thrilled with love’s sweet sickness, For she took delight in his breadth and height— But how she adored his thickness! So that poor little Square just died of despair, For his love he could not strangle; While the bold Cube led to the bridal bed That cute and acute Triangle. The Square’s sad lot she has long forgot, And his passionate pretensions ... For she dotes on her kids—Oh such cute Pyramids In a world of three dimensions.

> Who adored a fine Triangle;

### Option 2: Sophisticated Narrative Prose (Elegant Fable Style)
*This version transforms the light verse into an eloquent, fable-style narrative while preserving every detail.*

> Once in a geometric plane, there lived a tidy and modest Square who was hopelessly enamored with a charming, acute Triangle. Though she was a fickle flirt who kept him dangling in uncertainty, he remained undeterred by the prospect of domestic woes. He firmly believed it was his destiny to wed her and raise a family of delightful little Squares and Triangles.
> 
> His dreams were dashed the day a magnificent Cube swaggered onto their path. Carrying himself with an air of haughty superiority, the Cube effortlessly reduced the simple Square to an object of ridicule. The Triangle immediately fell under his solid spell, thrilled by the sweet pangs of love. While she admired his impressive height and breadth, it was his formidable thickness that truly captivated her heart.
> 
> Unable to quench his devotion, the poor Square perished of sheer despair. Meanwhile, the triumphant Cube led the charmingly acute Triangle to the altar. Long since unmindful of the Square’s tragic fate and ardent vows, she now dotes blissfully on their children—a house full of adorable Pyramids—thriving in a world of three dimensions.

**The Geometry of Heartbreak**

In the flat expanse of a two-dimensional world, a dependable Square fell deeply in love with a sharp and flirtatious Triangle. Captivated by her dynamic angles and charming turns, the Square envisioned a beautiful, orderly future together. He spent his days dreaming of the life they would build: a traditional union anchored by stability, culminating in a happy home and a family of little geometric shapes. 

However, the Square’s dreams were abruptly shattered by the arrival of a bold and magnificent Cube. Unlike anyone in their two-dimensional realm, the Cube possessed an astounding presence defined by three-dimensional breadth, height, and thick structural volume. The Triangle was instantly enthralled. Compared to the Cube’s breathtaking depth and grandeur, the Square’s simple, flat perspective suddenly seemed unremarkable.

Spurned in favor of the newcomer, the Square was crushed by the Triangle’s cold rejection. He found himself utterly incapable of letting go of the profound love he carried. Consumed by grief and unable to navigate a world devoid of the future he had envisioned, the Square slowly withered away, finally dying of sheer despair.

Unmoved by the tragedy left in her wake, the Triangle eagerly accepted the Cube’s proposal. Wrapped up in the excitement of her glamorous new life, she quickly forgot the Square's tender feelings and his tragic, lonely end. 

Leaving the flat plane behind, the Triangle and the Cube settled together into the vast expanse of the three-dimensional world. There, surrounded by endless depth and space, they built a prosperous life, happily raising a family of energetic Pyramid children who seamlessly combined the sharp triangular faces of their mother with the sturdy, volumetric bases of their father.
outputs.L4:
In the pristine, unbroken expanse of Flatland, where life was defined strictly by length and breadth, the Square considered himself a figure of exceptional stability. With four perfectly equal sides and four immaculate ninety-degree angles, he was a picture of middle-class geometric respectability. For months, his four perimeter lines had thrilled at the sight of a particular Isosceles Triangle. 

She was a breathtaking creature—sharp, dynamic, and hopelessly flirtatious. Her acute angle swept through the planar streets with a dangerous, alluring charm. To the Square, she was the apex of beauty.

One afternoon, beneath the uniform light of their two-dimensional world, the Square finally summoned the courage to press his suit. He approached her along a straight axis, keeping his edges neatly aligned. 

"My dear Triangle," the Square began, his perimeter trembling with earnest devotion. "I offer you a life of perfect symmetry. Together, we can enclose a area of pure, unyielding harmony. My right angles will forever shield you from the chaos of irregular polygons."

The Triangle rotated teasingly, her sharp point catching the ambient light. "A square is so very predictable," she purred, sliding a fraction of an inch closer. "Four sides, always identical. Where is the excitement? Where is the danger?"

Yet, she did not walk away. She lingered, enjoying the devotion of so solid a suitor. The Square felt victory within his reach. He began to recite a poem about the elegance of right angles, convinced that his steadfastness would win her heart.

Then, the world warped.

It did not happen along the north, south, east, or west axes. Instead, a strange, suffocating pressure pressed down upon the very fabric of their plane. Suddenly, an impossibility materialized before them. It began as a tiny, dense line, rapidly expanding into a pristine square—yet it did not move through the space of Flatland. It seemed to grow out of nowhere, shifting and morphing with breathtaking fluidity.

It was a Cube. 

To the flat inhabitants, he appeared as a shimmering, impossible entity, capable of seeing not just their boundaries, but their very insides. But when the Cube projected his voice, it reverberated from a mysterious direction that was neither left nor right. 

"Greetings, creatures of the flat," the Cube boomed, his voice rich with volumetric resonance. 

The Square recoiled, his angles tightening in alarm. But the Triangle was instantly spellbound. 

The Cube, sensing her fascination, began to showcase his magnificence. He did not merely slide along the plane; he *passed through* it. To the Triangle’s wide-eyed wonder, the stranger altered his visible cross-section at will, revealing shifting internal areas of staggering complexity. 

"You live in a prison of two dimensions," the Cube whispered, turning his attention entirely to the flirtatious Triangle. "You know only length and width. But I possess *depth*. I hold volume. I inhabit the majestic realm of 'Upward'—a direction your simple suitor cannot even fathom."

The Cube effortlessly flexed his twelve edges and eight vertices, casting a shadow of sheer structural superiority over the flat landscape. Compared to this godlike titan of space, the Square suddenly looked impossibly dull—a flat, rigid coaster of a shape with nothing hidden beneath his surface.

"Take me with you," the Triangle breathed, completely enamored by the Cube’s glorious stature and unseen dimensions. "Show me this... 'Upward'."

"No!" the Square cried out, attempting to slide his body between them. "He is an illusion! A mathematical absurdity! I have four true angles—I am solid!"

"You are flat," the Cube dismissed coolly. With a gentle, three-dimensional lift, the Cube reached *down* into Flatland, touching the Triangle’s interior—a sensation so intimate and profound that she gasped. 

With a final, pitying glance at the desperate Square, the Cube lifted the Triangle slightly out of the plane, bending the rules of reality to sweep her away into his volumetric paradise.

Left behind on the cold, flat surface, the Square stood frozen. He watched the point where she had vanished, waiting for her to return to the only world that made sense. But she did not. 

The agony of rejection shattered the Square’s rigid composure. His mind could not reconcile the loss, nor could his geometry endure the humiliation of his planar limitations. Slowly, his precise right angles began to warp. His straight edges buckled under the weight of an unrequited love he had no axis to measure. Within hours, his structural integrity collapsed completely. The Square withered, his area shrinking to a microscopic point, until he died of a profoundly broken heart.

Far above the flat plane, in the vast and shimmering expanse of the Third Dimension, the Triangle and the Cube were united. Their union defied the simple laws of Flatland, producing offspring that carried the legacy of both worlds: majestic Pyramids. Rising from flat, sharp bases into glorious three-dimensional peaks, these children stood as eternal monuments to their father's depth—a stark, unyielding proof of the ultimate triumph of higher-dimensional existence over a flat and simple life.

Every city has a place that serves as its beating heart, **and** for this small mountain village, it was the central market plaza. Right **there**, beneath the shadow of the old clock tower, lay a perfectly paved stone **square**. 

During the day, vendors set up colorful wooden stalls filled with fresh produce, handmade ceramics, **and** aromatic spices. Children chased pigeons across the smooth flags, their laughter echoing off the historic brick facades. 

As evening fell, soft yellow streetlamps hummed to life, **and** the space transformed. Couples walked hand in hand, stopping to listen to the street musicians whose melodies floated through the cool air. Standing **there** in the quiet after dusk, watching the stars appear above the geometric lines of the **square**, one couldn't help but feel a profound sense of peace **and** belonging.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny narrative poem about a love triangle involving literal geometric shapes.
counterfactuals.output:
In Plane Geometry Town, where the gridlines are neat,
Lived Barnaby Square, who was rigid and sweet.
He had four equal sides, ninety-degree grace,
And a wonderfully predictable, box-shaped embrace.

He was madly in love with a girl named Polyne,
A right-angled triangle, sharp and divine.
Her hypotenuse dazzled, her base was secure,
And her angles added up to one-eighty, for sure.

Barnaby wooed her with grid paper sheets:
"Oh Polly," he begged, "we’d make marvelous sweets!
If we stick side-by-side, we can build a fine prism,
Forget all the chaos of modernism!"

Polly smiled, quite acute, though a little bit split,
For she wasn't quite sure if the Square was a fit.
Barnaby’s logic was sturdy and sound,
But she secretly longed for a shape more *round*.

Then into the graph paper district there rolled
Sir Cecil the Circle, charismatic and bold!
With no corners, no edges, just pure $2\pi r$,
He cruised through the axes like a classic sports car.

He spun up to Polly and whispered with gleam,
"That Square is too rigid, he lives in a scheme!
He’s boxed in his thinking, his life is a chore,
Come roll with me, baby, and see something more!

My area’s vast, and my curves never end,
Why stay with a guy who can’t even bend?"
Polly shivered and blushed to her very top peak;
A smooth operator had made her knees weak.

Well, Barnaby saw them! His perimeter shook!
He marched over quickly with a menacing look.
"Get away from my girl!" yelled the Square with a frown.
"You’re a rolling disaster! The joke of this town!"

"You're *pointless*!" roared Barnaby, red in the face.
"You’re just spinning your wheels all over the place!"
"At least," laughed the Circle, "I’m smooth and refined!
Your head is so boxy, you’ve lost your whole mind!"

"Your value is *irrational*!" Barnaby cried.
"And your perimeter’s dull!" Cecil quickly replied.
They argued in tangents, they bickered in sine,
Crossing every coordinate, boundary, and line.

Poor Polly stood caught in the heat of the fight,
Stuck right in the middle—obtuse, or acute, or just right?
"Oh dear," sobbed the Triangle, weeping in math,
"I’m trapped in a tragic, isosceles path!

Is it right to choose Square? Is it wrong to love Pi?
I’m a Love Triangle now!" she released a great sigh.
Then she looked at the boys, who were throwing big fits,
Tearing graph paper town into literal bits.

She yelled, "Gentlemen, stop! I have drawn the last line!
I refuse to be claimed as a piece of design!
Barnaby, you are too stiff and controlled!
Cecil, you’re smooth, but you constantly roll!"

So she left them both standing at $X$ equals zero,
And went off to find her own personal hero.
Now she lives on the beach, doing fine on her own,
The sharpest young shape that has ever been known.

And the moral is simple, for lovers of math:
When a triangle’s love takes a treacherous path,
Don't get boxed in by squares, don't go running in rings—
Just stick to your angles, and see what life brings!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose a playful rhyming story where a 2D Square loses the love of a Triangle to a bold 3D Cube? Include puns on terms like "acute" and "thickness."
counterfactuals.output:
In the Land of the Grid, where the paper was flat,  
Lived Simon the Square, looking sharp where he sat.  
He had four equal sides and four angles so *right*,  
And he loved Little Trixie with all of his might.  

Now, Trixie was pointed, a Triangle fine,  
With a slope that was sleek and a stylish baseline.  
Simon wooed her with compliments, sweet and astute:  
“Oh Trixie,” he’d whisper, “you’re so very *acute*!”  
She would giggle and blush from her tip to her base,  
As they drew little hearts on their two-D surface.  

Then out from the depth of the Z-axis line,  
Rolled a shadowy stranger of solid design!  
’Twas Chad, a bold Cube from a world multi-layered,  
And next to his volume, poor Simon felt scared.  
Chad didn’t just lie on the X and the Y,  
He popped off the page! He was six-faced and sly!  

“Hey baby,” flexed Chad, “leave this flat little clown.  
I’ve got depth, I’ve got space, I’m the talk of the town!”  
Poor Trixie was dazzled; her vertices shook  
At the *thickness* he flexed in a single side-look.  
“He has volume!” she gasped. “He’s got shaded-in weight!  
Simon, I’m sorry, but this is my fate.”  

“Wait!” Simon protested. “I’m predictable! Fair!  
I’ve got ninety degrees! I’m a marvelous square!”  
But Trixie just sighed, “Simon, don’t be *obtuse*,  
Your two-D proportion is no longer of use.  
You’re just far too *plane*, lacking shadow and grace,  
While Chad takes up real three-dimensional space!”  

So Trixie bounced off with the block of her dreams,  
Leaving poor Little Simon to burst at his seams.  
He felt broken and flat, stripped of all of his pride,  
With a tear dripping down from his top-leftmost side.  

Yet Simon survived, though his heartbreak was vast,  
He knew that a fad like a 3D would pass.  
Now he searches the grid for a sweetheart that’s true—  
Maybe a Circle or Rhombus will do!  
For though he lacks depth, Simon knows he’s still *right*,  
And a flat, equal lover will suit him just fine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Poem about shapes falling in love.
counterfactuals.output:
The Square had lived in ninety degrees,
With rigid bounds and equal sides.
He counted corners, felt at ease,
Where strict, predictable logic hides.

Then rolled the Circle into view,
Without an edge, without a start,
An endless loop of dynamic hue,
With infinite *pi* inside her heart.

He feared her roll would break his frame;
She feared his points might cut her curve.
They were not built to be the same,
Yet felt a force they didn't deserve.

She rested gently on his side—
A single tangent, soft and slight.
His sharpest corners opened wide;
Her endless motion found its light.

He gave her anchor, base, and ground,
A place to rest her spinning soul.
In his static lines, a peace she found;
In her soft bend, he felt made whole.

No longer trapped by grid or plane,
They fit where math could not define:
A circle wrapped in a square’s domain,
Two distant worlds in one design. 

For love is not in matching angles,
Nor in perimeters aligned,
But how two different shapes untangle
The perfect form they leave behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lighthearted ballad in the style of humorous narrative verse about a 2D square who gets dumped for a 3-dimensional cube. Make sure they have pyramid children at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
Oh, Sammy was a simple shape, as flat as flat could be,
With four right angles, equal sides, existing in 2D.
He lived upon a grid of graph, contented with his lot—
A cozy, two-dimensional piece of paper on a plot.

He fell in love with Trixie, a triangle so acute,
With three sharp points, three slender lines, and undeniably cute.
They strolled along the X and Y, beneath a poly-sky,
And swore their flat, Euclidean love would never, ever die.

But then strutted Chester Cube, a flashy 3D swell,
Who sauntered off the Z-axis with volume he could sell.
He boasted of his six solid faces, bright and bold,
And eight impressive vertices of three-D solid gold!

Poor Trixie’s head was turned at once by Chester’s glossy frame;
She looked at Sammy’s paper life and said, "You are too tame!
I need a man with *depth*, my dear—a true volumetric hero!
While your Z-axis measurement is stuck at absolute zero!"

She dumped poor Sammy on the spot and left him on the page,
While Sammy crumpled in the dirt in two-dimensional rage.
"I’m just a flat, deflated plane!" he whimpered in despair,
"A square without a third dimension isn’t anywhere!"

But Chester Cube was bulky, and he took up way too space;
He couldn't slide through narrow slots, he crushed the drawing space!
He knocked down all the furniture, he couldn't fold or bend,
And Trixie realized "depth" was just a hassle in the end.

She ran right back to Sammy, shedding tears of pure regret:
"Oh, Sammy, you’re the *right-est* angle that I’ve ever met!
Forgive my foolish wandering, I miss your sturdy base!"
And Sammy opened up his arms and offered an embrace.

They combined their forms together, X and Y and Z for fun,
For when a Square and Triangle decide that they are one—
With a flat square foundation and triangular walls so grand,
They built a three-D family across the graph-paper land!

Now little baby Pyramids go bouncing down the hall,
With square-shaped bottoms, pointy tops, the proudest of them all!
So if you’re flat, don’t lose your heart when 3D rivals show:
A humble square can raise a peak and make a kingdom grow!
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a silly math-themed poem that uses a romantic melodrama to contrast two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon the graph paper, crisp and neat,  
Where X and Y in passion meet,  
Swooned Lady Circle, thin and flat—  
No depth, no height, just *that was that*.  

Then stepped Sir Cube into her sight,  
Extravagant in shade and light!  
He bowed and brushed her tangent line:  
“Oh, Lady Circle, be my sine!”  

“My love!” she swooned. “My area’s small,  
Yet you’re the grandest of them all!  
Our love is bounded, pure, and true!”  
…Until he shifted out of view.  

He popped *upward*—a scandalous flex!  
A movement far beyond the X!  
She gasped, she shrieked, she clutched her chart:  
“What witchcraft tears my plane apart?!”  

“Forgive me, babe!” he cried in pain,  
“I am too thick for just one plane!  
I have a Z-axis! I’ve got *depth*!  
A secret height! A shaded breadth!”  

“You monster!” wailed the flat young lass,  
“You hypocrite of spatial class!  
I thought you were a square like me,  
Not hiding volume... in *3D*!”  

“When you pass through, you pretend you’re flat!  
A sliced-up fraud in a fancy hat!  
To me, you’re just a cross-section square,  
While hiding faces in the air!”  

“I offered length! I offered width!”  
He wept, “Yet volume is my myth!  
We cannot wed, we cannot mate—  
The third dimension seals our fate!”  

“Farewell!” he sobbed, and rose on high,  
Up to the Z-axis in the sky.  
She stayed below, forever flat,  
Where only two dimensions sat,  

Tracing her tears upon the chart—  
A zero-volume, broken heart.
